<reason>Side A (CON) won a tight, high-quality exchange. B's best weapon—the coherence flip that A's own alternative (cash/respite/services) requires the same verification A calls impossible—was genuinely damaging, but A answered it with a real distinction of kind: a revocable, needs-based payment whose error "dies with the payment" versus a vested, compounding claim collected from contributors who never entered that household. B's counter that this is "degree, not kind" was asserted more than argued. On cost, B's margin response contained a logical gap A exposed: if most care happens anyway, the credit is behaviorally inert but fiscally vast, and B never resolved the aggregate liability or A's targeting critique (credits vesting in non-poor second earners). B also mischaracterized the closing by claiming A "never told us" why the two columns differ when A5.4 answered it directly, and B suffered two clipped turns (opening and rebuttal 2), an execution cost. Both sides used A1/A2 format properly and the pressure questions were sharp on both sides.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B3.1's trap—your alternative needs the verification you call impossible—was the most decisive pressure of the debate, and A4.1-A4.2's answer (a time-limited benefit tolerates a rough gate because the error dies with the payment; a contribution year compounds and vests) was the most decisive reply, preserving A's core distinction and surviving B's "degree not kind" rejoinder.</best_rebuttal>
